text:
patchwork

Plots are combined with a +

Add a general title with plot_annotation(title = "...")
Add a general subtitle with plot_annotation(subtitle = "...")
Change the formatting with plot_annotation(theme = theme(plot.title = element_text(...)))



Code
library(patchwork)
# Two example plots
p1 <- ggplot(mtcars, aes(x = hp, y = mpg)) +
  geom_point(color = "steelblue", size = 3, alpha = 0.7) +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(title = "Fuel efficiency vs Horsepower")

p2 <- ggplot(mtcars, aes(x = factor(cyl), y = mpg)) +
  geom_boxplot(fill = "steelblue", alpha = 0.7) +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(title = "MPG by Number of Cylinders") +
  theme(legend.position = "none")

# Combine with patchwork and add title
combined <- p1 + p2 +
  plot_annotation(
    title = "Analysis of mtcars dataset",
    subtitle = paste(
      "Exploring relationships between engine features",
      "and fuel efficiency"
    ),
    caption = "Data source: mtcars",
    theme = theme(
      plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 16),
      plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 14)
    )
  )

Font embedding
Vector images pick the closest font available (if the actual font is not available on the recipients computer). You can embed fonts into the vector image.

showtext converts characters into polygons. Embedding is no longer required, but text is no longer searchable.
extrafont supports font embedding, but supports fewer fonts.

Adobe Acrobat (paid version) can be used to manually embed fonts in a PDF.

Packages: showtext, extrafont.

title: Quickstart: the DUO Data & ggplot Basics
section: Part 1 — Load and inspect the data
text:
Part 1 — Load and inspect the data
We’ll focus on one of those four files, eindscores. This shows the average transfer test score per primary school, broken down by which of the six test providers (IEP, Route8, DIA, AMN, DOE, LIB) that school used.

library(tidyverse)

eindscores <- read_delim(
  "data/raw/eindscores_2024-2025.csv",
  delim = ";", # DUO's files are ;-separated
  # NL uses , as decimal point
  locale = locale(decimal_mark = ",", encoding = "UTF-8"),
  show_col_types = FALSE
)

Run glimpse(eindscores) yourself and notice the shape: one row per school, with a separate pair of columns per provider — IEP_AANTAL/IEP_GEM, ROUTE8_AANTAL/ROUTE8_GEM, and so on (AANTAL = number of students tested, GEM = their average score). Most schools use exactly one provider, so five of those six AANTAL columns will be 0 for any given row.

Quickstart: the DUO Data & ggplot Basics
text:
Part 3 — ggplot basics
Every ggplot2 plot answers three questions: what data, which variables map to which visual properties (aes()), and what shape represents each observation (a geom, added with +).
ggplot(data = <DATASET>, mapping = aes(<AESTHETIC MAPPINGS>)) +
  geom_<SOMETHING>()

Exercise 1 — Your first plot
geom_bar() counts rows for you automatically — perfect for “how many schools use each provider?”

Try itPlotSolution


ggplot(school_provider, aes(x = ____)) +
  geom_____()






ggplot(school_provider, aes(x = provider)) +
  geom_bar()






Exercise 2 — Mapping vs. setting
An aesthetic mapped to a variable goes inside aes() and varies per observation; an aesthetic just set to a fixed value goes outside aes(). Fix the mistake below (it’s trying to make every bar steelblue, but puts the color where a mapping would go), then extend it to map fill to provider instead.

Try itPlotSolution



ggplot(school_provider, aes(x = provider, fill = "steelblue")) +
  geom_bar()







# fix: "steelblue" must be set, not mapped
ggplot(school_provider, aes(x = provider)) +
  geom_bar(fill = "steelblue")

# extended: fill mapped to a variable instead
ggplot(school_provider, aes(x = provider, fill = provider)) +
  geom_bar()






Picking a geom for the question you’re asking







Question
Reach for




How do two continuous variables relate?
geom_point()


How does a value compare across categories?
geom_col() / geom_bar()*


How is a continuous variable distributed?
geom_histogram()


How does a distribution differ across groups?
geom_boxplot()



*geom_bar() counts rows for you; geom_col() expects you to already have a column of heights to plot (like n_students).


Exercise 3 — A different geom
Plot the distribution of n_students across all schools with a histogram.

Try itPlotSolution


ggplot(school_provider, aes(x = ____)) +
  geom_____()






ggplot(school_provider, aes(x = n_students)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 5)






Labels, themes, colors

labs() controls text: title, axis titles, legend title.

scale_fill_manual() / scale_color_manual() control colors: here, I show you how to map specific values to specific colors with a named vector. You can also do this with pre-defined color scaling, with functions such as scale_fill_viridis() (try it with scale_fill_viridis_d()!)
theme_*() controls overall look: theme_minimal(), theme_bw(), etc.
Inside theme() you can also tweak your own styling. I’ve added a few common features in the code below.


# one fixed color per provider, so it stays the same across every plot you make
provider_colors <- c(
  LIB = "#2a78d6", IEP = "#eb6834", ROUTE8 = "#1baf7a",
  DIA = "#4a3aa7", AMN = "#e87ba4", DOE = "#eda100"
)

ggplot(school_provider, aes(x = provider, fill = provider)) +
  geom_bar() +
  scale_fill_manual(values = provider_colors) +
  labs(
    title = "Schools per transfer test provider",
    x = "Provider",
    y = "Number of schools",
    fill = "Provider",
    caption = "Figure 1. \nNumber of schools per transfer test provider"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    # ggplot right-aligns captions by default - this centers it
    plot.caption = element_text(hjust = 0.5),
    # change font sizes and family with the element_text() argument
    plot.title = element_text(size = 16, face = "bold", family = "courier"),
    legend.position = "top", # use legend.postion = "none" to remove the legend
    panel.grid.major.x = element_blank()
  ) # remove grid lines in background








Facets

facet_wrap() splits one plot into a panel per category of a variable — instead of cramming every group into one plot with color, you get a small multiple per group, each with its own axes.
facet_grid() does something similar, but arranges panels into a fixed grid (rows × columns) instead of wrapping them into however many rows/columns fit.
Once each panel is already labeled by the variable, a color legend for that same variable is redundant — theme(legend.position = "none") drops it.
The facet labels themselves (the little strip above each panel) are also styled through theme(): strip.text for the label text, strip.background for the strip behind it, and panel.spacing for the gap between panels. For an easy option, using theme_bw() already styles facets nicely.


ggplot(school_provider, aes(x = provider, fill = provider)) +
  geom_bar() +
  # the same named vector from above
  scale_fill_manual(values = provider_colors) +
  # use scales = "free_x", "free_y, or "free" to rescale the axis per facet
  facet_wrap(~PROVINCIE) +
  labs(
    x = "Provider", y = "Number of schools",
    title = "Schools per transfer test provider, by province"
  ) +
  # theme_bw() already styles facets nicely, in my opinion. but see options in
  # theme() below for how to customize it yourself!
  theme_bw() +
  theme(
    legend.position = "none",
    axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1),
    # facet label text
    strip.text = element_text(face = "bold", size = 10, color = "white"),
    # facet label background
    strip.background = element_rect(fill = "steelblue4", color = NA),
    panel.spacing = unit(1, "lines")
  ) # space between panels

title: Build an interactive viz with ggplotly
text:
This handout shows a way to use ggplotly() to build an interactive map: one point per school, colored by which transfer test provider it used, and a hover tooltip. Here, the ggplotly() mechanics are applied to coordinates. In assignment 1, you’ll apply it to simple x/y points on a scatter plot.
library(tidyverse)
library(plotly) # turns a ggplot into an interactive widget

title: Build an interactive viz with ggplotly
text:
Getting the data
You already have eindscores if you’ve done the ggplot recap worksheet - see its Setup section for data/get-data.R. For this map we need one more thing DUO doesn’t give us directly: coordinates. eindscores only has each school’s postcode (POSTCODE_VESTIGING), not a latitude/longitude.
We’ll use 4PP (MIT licensed), an open lookup table of the centroid coordinates for every Dutch 4-digit postcode area. Download it once:

download.file(
  "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/bobdenotter/4pp/master/4pp.csv",
  # where to save it locally, alongside the other course data
  destfile = "data/raw/postcodes_pc4.csv",
  mode = "wb" # "write binary" - avoids a corrupted file on Windows
)

title: Build an interactive viz with ggplotly
text:
Prepare the data
Same school_provider shape as the ggplot recap worksheet, but this time we keep POSTCODE_VESTIGING around so we have something to join the coordinates on. DUO’s postcodes are 6 characters (e.g. "2716PH"); the coordinate lookup only goes down to the first 4 digits (a postcode area, not an exact address) - close enough to place a school on a map of the whole country.

eindscores <- read_delim(
  "data/raw/eindscores_2024-2025.csv",
  delim = ";", # DUO's files are ;-separated, not comma-separated
  # NL uses , as the decimal point
  locale = locale(decimal_mark = ",", encoding = "UTF-8"),
  show_col_types = FALSE
)

postcodes <- read_csv("data/raw/postcodes_pc4.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  # a few postcodes appear more than once in this file - keep just one row per
  # postcode
  distinct(postcode, .keep_all = TRUE) |>
  # we only need these three columns for the join below
  select(postcode, latitude, longitude)

school_provider <- eindscores |>
  # keep just the school identifiers/labels, the postcode, and the six
  # *_AANTAL columns (number of students tested, per provider)
  select(
    INSTELLINGSCODE, VESTIGINGSCODE, INSTELLINGSNAAM_VESTIGING,
    GEMEENTENAAM, PROVINCIE, POSTCODE_VESTIGING, ends_with("_AANTAL")
  ) |>
  # stack the six AANTAL columns into two: which provider, how many students -
  # turns "one row per school, six provider columns" into "one row per
  # (school, provider), with n_students telling us how many students it tested"
  pivot_longer(
    cols = ends_with("_AANTAL"),
    names_to = "provider",
    values_to = "n_students"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    provider = sub("_AANTAL$", "", provider), # e.g. IEP_AANTAL becomes IEP
    # DUO writes "<5" for small counts -> this becomes NA
    n_students = as.numeric(n_students),
    # keep only the numeric part: "2716PH" -> 2716
    postcode = as.numeric(str_sub(POSTCODE_VESTIGING, 1, 4))
  ) |>
  # drop the providers a school didn't actually use
  filter(!is.na(n_students), n_students > 0) |>
  # group the rows back up by school...
  group_by(INSTELLINGSCODE, VESTIGINGSCODE) |>
  # ...and keep only its single largest provider (most schools use just one
  # anyway)
  slice_max(n_students, n = 1, with_ties = FALSE) |>
  ungroup()

# join the coordinates onto each school by matching postcode -> postcode.
# inner_join() only keeps rows that find a match in BOTH tables, so a
# school whose postcode isn't in the lookup table gets dropped here - in
# practice this matches ~99.9% of schools, so barely any are lost
school_map <- school_provider |>
  inner_join(postcodes, by = "postcode")

title: Build an interactive viz with ggplotly
text:
Build the plot
Here, we make a very simple map visualization with points. To do this, we use coord_fixed() with a latitude correction. Real map projections usually use polygon boundaries (country/province outlines); to make these more complex map visualizations, coord_map() or geom_sf() can be used. However ggplotly()‘s support for geom_sf() is known to be inconsistent (tooltips and rendering can break). Here, coord_fixed() gets us a correctly-proportioned map with none of that risk. The ratio below (1 / cos(latitude)) corrects for the Netherlands’ latitude, so the country doesn’t look horizontally stretched.
Feel free to explore more complex map visualizations on your own, with more complex interactive viz tools such as leaflet (the standard for interactive maps in R - real basemaps, polygons, markers, popups) or plotly’s own native mapping functions (plot_ly(type = "choroplethmapbox"), plot_geo()).

provider_colors <- c(
  LIB = "#2a78d6", IEP = "#eb6834", ROUTE8 = "#1baf7a",
  DIA = "#4a3aa7", AMN = "#e87ba4", DOE = "#eda100"
)

nl_map <- ggplot(
  school_map,
  aes(x = longitude, y = latitude, color = provider)
) +
  # alpha < 1 so overlapping points show up as darker patches
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5, size = 1.2) +
  scale_color_manual(values = provider_colors) +
  # keep the map's proportions correct - NL sits at ~52.1°N
  coord_fixed(ratio = 1 / cos(52.1 * pi / 180)) +
  labs(
    title = "Schools by transfer test provider",
    color = "Provider",
    x = NULL,
    y = NULL
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    # hide the lat/long numbers - not meaningful to a reader
    axis.text = element_blank(),
    axis.ticks = element_blank(),
    panel.grid = element_blank() # hide gridlines
  )

nl_map

title: Build an interactive viz with ggplotly
text:
Make it interactive
Same pattern as the other ggplotly() example: add a text aesthetic with whatever you want the tooltip to show, then wrap the plot in ggplotly(..., tooltip = "text").

nl_map_interactive <- ggplot(
  school_map,
  aes(
    x = longitude, y = latitude, color = provider,
    # build the tooltip text ourselves, one string per row - this is what
    # shows up when someone hovers over a point. <b> and <br> are HTML tags
    # plotly understands, for bold text and line breaks
    text = paste0(
      "<b>", INSTELLINGSNAAM_VESTIGING, "</b>",
      "<br>", GEMEENTENAAM, ", ", PROVINCIE,
      "<br>Provider: ", provider,
      "<br>students tested: ", n_students
    )
  )
) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5, size = 1.2) +
  scale_color_manual(values = provider_colors) +
  coord_fixed(ratio = 1 / cos(52.1 * pi / 180)) +
  labs(
    title = "Schools by transfer test provider",
    color = "Provider",
    x = NULL,
    y = NULL
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    axis.text = element_blank(),
    axis.ticks = element_blank(),
    panel.grid = element_blank()
  )

# convert the static ggplot into an interactive plotly widget;
# tooltip = "text" shows our custom text column on hover
ggplotly(nl_map_interactive, tooltip = "text")



Zoom, pan, and hover over a few points - notice how the providers cluster regionally rather than being scattered evenly across the country.

This page gives you the background you need to understand the data, a codebook for every file, and a list of pitfalls to watch out for.
You don’t need to be Dutch, or know anything about the Dutch education system, to work with this data. You do need the handful of terms below, because they show up directly as column names and category labels.

title: The DUO Data: Background & Codebook
text:
Background

The Dutch school system, just enough of it
Dutch primary school (basisonderwijs, PO) runs from groep 1 to groep 8, roughly ages 4 to 12. Most students attend a regular primary school (Bo); students who need extra support may attend a special primary school (Sbo, speciaal basisonderwijs).
At the end of groep 8, every student gets a school advice (schooladvies): the secondary-school (voortgezet onderwijs, VO) track that the student should go to. From the most practical to the most academic:








Track
Full name
What it is




PRO
praktijkonderwijs
practical education, for students who need the most support


VMBO-B
basisberoepsgerichte leerweg
preparatory vocational education, basic track


VMBO-K
kaderberoepsgerichte leerweg
preparatory vocational education, “framework” track


VMBO-GT
gemengde/theoretische leerweg
preparatory vocational education, mixed/theoretical track


HAVO
hoger algemeen voortgezet onderwijs
senior general secondary education


VWO
voorbereidend wetenschappelijk onderwijs
pre-university education



There is also VSO (voortgezet speciaal onderwijs), special-needs secondary education, which sits outside this ranking. A student can also get a combined advice, like VMBO-GT/HAVO, when the school thinks either track could fit.
The track a student starts in matters a lot: switching tracks later is possible, but not easy. This is why the advice, and everything that feeds into it, is a sensitive topic.


What is a doorstroomtoets?
Near the end of groep 8 (around February), every student takes a doorstroomtoets (“transfer test”; doorstroom = “flow-through”, toets = “test”). It is a standardized test of reading, language and maths. Its main purpose is to be an objective second opinion next to the teacher’s judgement: if a student scores higher than their teacher’s advice suggests, the school must reconsider (heroverweging) the advice. In principle, the advice can only be adjusted upwards.
The doorstroomtoets replaced the old eindtoets (“final test”, including the well-known Citotoets) from the 2023–2024 school year. Since then, schools can choose which doorstroomtoets their students take, from six approved providers:









Code in the data
Test
Publisher
Notes




LIB
Leerling in Beeld
Cito B.V.
successor of the old Citotoets; used by almost half of all schools


IEP
IEP Eindtoets
Bureau ICE
used by about 40% of schools


ROUTE8
Route 8
A-VISION
digital and adaptive


DIA
Dia-Eindtoets
Diataal BV



AMN
AMN Eindtoets
AMN B.V.



DOE
Overheidsdoorstroomtoets
Stichting Cito
the free, government-funded test; used by less than 1% of schools



Each provider reports its scores on its own scale, so an IEP score of 80 and a LIB score of 180 can’t be compared. To make the tests comparable, all results are also translated into reference levels (referentieniveaus): standardized skill levels that are meant to mean the same thing, whichever test a student took.

1F (fundamenteel niveau): the basic level, which nearly every student should reach.
1S (maths) and 2F (reading and language): the higher target level (streefniveau).



The fairness debate
The idea behind letting schools choose was that all six tests are equivalent. A series of investigations by the newspaper de Volkskrant, starting in January 2025, found that they are not:

Reference levels differ by provider. For example, about 49% of students who took Route 8 reached reading level 2F, compared to about 80% of students who took the paper version of LIB. In maths, students who took LIB reached level 1S about twice as often as students who took Route 8.
School advice differs by provider, even more starkly. students who took AMN got a PRO or VMBO-B advice about 18 times as often as students who took paper LIB (14.6% vs. 0.8%). Paper LIB students got a VWO advice 15.4% of the time, AMN students 4.4%.
This is not (only) because different kinds of schools choose different tests. The obvious objection is that schools don’t choose a provider at random. Maybe schools with more disadvantaged students happen to prefer certain tests. The Volkskrant therefore compared schools with an equal schoolweging (a measure of how disadvantaged a school’s student population is, see the codebook). The gap between providers remained. In other words, it’s partly a property of the test itself.
Test format matters too. According to the College voor Toetsen en Examens (CvTE), which oversees the tests, 77% of students with a VWO teacher advice got a VWO test result on the paper LIB test, compared to 43% on the digital IEP test.

Critics called the doorstroomtoets an “ongelijkheidsmachine” (“inequality machine”): a test that was introduced to make educational opportunities more equal might be doing the opposite. Reporting on the 2026 results found that the gaps between providers had narrowed somewhat, but not disappeared. Schools with a more disadvantaged population also adjust their advice more often than other schools.
Where things stand. Sector organisations (PO-Raad, VO-raad) and the Dutch parliament pushed for a single national test. On 2 July 2026, the State Secretary for Education announced a plan to go from six providers back to one national doorstroomtoets by school year 2029/2030, stating that “full comparability is a utopia”: every difference in test design shifts the results.






Note



The numbers above come from the Volkskrant, CvTE and other sources (see Sources), which had access to student-level data. The DUO files you work with are school-level: you know how many students at a school reached each level, and which provider the school used, but not the results of individual students. Keep this in mind when you draw conclusions.

title: The DUO Data: Background & Codebook
text:
Codebook
All files contain data from the 2024–2025 school year, with one row per school location. The three DUO files (eindscores, referentieniveaus, schooladviezen) share the same identifying columns; schoolweging comes from a different organisation and is structured differently.






"<5" means “fewer than 5”



To protect students’ privacy, DUO hides every count below 5 and writes the text "<5" instead. This means that count columns are read into R as text, not numbers, and as.numeric() silently turns every "<5" into NA. See Pitfalls for how to deal with this.



Identifying columns (all DUO files)







Column
Meaning




PEILDATUM_LEERLINGEN / PEILDATUM
reference date for the student counts (1 October 2024)


PRIKDATUM
date the data was extracted


INSTELLINGSCODE
school code (also known as the “BRIN” code), the school’s main ID


VESTIGINGSCODE
location code: which building, if a school has more than one


INSTELLINGSNAAM_VESTIGING
name of the school (location)


POSTCODE_VESTIGING
postal code


PLAATSNAAM
town or city


GEMEENTENUMMER / GEMEENTENAAM
municipality code / name


PROVINCIE
province (the Netherlands has 12)


SOORT_PO
school type: Bo (regular primary) or Sbo (special primary)

title: The DUO Data: Background & Codebook
text:
Tips
Look out for these features in the data:

One row is one school, not one student. Every number is a count or average for a whole school. A school with 10 students in groep 8 counts as one row, just like a school with 100. Think about whether you want to weigh schools by their number of students, and be careful with conclusions about individual students.
Hidden counts ("<5"). Convert these explicitly instead of letting as.numeric() turn them into NA. In eindscores this affects only a few percent of schools. In referentieniveaus and schooladviezen it affects the large majority of schools, because students are split over many small categories, so dropping those schools is not an option. A reasonable approach is to replace "<5" with 2.5 (the midpoint of 1–4) and check whether your conclusion changes when you use 1 or 4 instead.
Wide format. eindscores has a pair of columns per provider, instead of one “provider” column. Use pivot_longer() to get one row per school per provider, and keep the provider with the most students (about 96% of schools use exactly one provider). See Worksheet 1 for a worked example.
Different score scales. Only compare providers on reference levels or school advice, never on the raw _GEM scores.

title: Working with Git
text:
Introduction
This tutorial walks you through how to get you started with Git, which you need to use for your group project.
Before you start, make sure you have a GitHub account and that Git is installed on your computer. You can check the second part in RStudio: go to Tools > Global Options > Git/SVN. If the Git executable field shows a path, you’re good to go. If it’s empty, install Git first (instructions), then restart RStudio.

title: Working with Git
text:
Repo structure
Your group repo should look like this (this template is available in templates/assignment-2/):
your-project-name/
├── .gitignore
├── README.md
├── your-project-name.Rproj
├── scripts/
│   ├── 00-packages.R
│   └── 01-get-data.R
└── report/
    └── DV-Assignment2-GroupX.Rmd

scripts/00-packages.R — installs (if missing) and loads every package the project uses.
scripts/01-get-data.R — downloads/loads the DUO data your group is using.
All external R scripts used to build dataframes, visualizations, etc, and are sourced for your final report, belong in scripts/. Use logical naming conventions here.

report/ — your group’s report and final visualization.

README is a short, summarized description of your project goals and outcomes. You can also use this file to guide readers through your speciifc files, and how to run them.

.gitignore is a list of all files that won’t be git-tracked. Make sure you ignore data/ — even though we work with public data, it is good practice to never push data to github. This data is always reproducible by re-running 01-get-data.R, so a copy in version control is not necessary.

This is based on the reproducible workflows described in Telling Stories with Data. We expect you to stick to this workflow and structure throughout the assignment. Points can be deducted if it is not clear which script we should run, and how.

title: Working with Git
text:
Connecting GitHub to RStudio

Step 1: Adding git-tracked R projects

Go to your group’s GitHub repository and click on the green <> Code button. Choose to clone the repository via HTTPS and copy the URL.

Now go to RStudio. On the top right (sort of cubical icon) you can find a project overview Project: (none). Make sure this is in fact set to no project, if you see the name of a different repository/project, click it and select Close Project.

Make a new R project for your group assignment: click on New Project > Version Control > Git. Paste the URL you just copied from GitHub into Repository URL, choose where on your computer the project should live, and create the project (the Project directory name will automatically be filled in for you).

















The first time you do this, RStudio may ask for your GitHub username and password. GitHub does not accept your normal password here - use a personal access token instead. You can create one on GitHub under Settings > Developer settings > Personal access tokens > Tokens (classic) > Generate new token (classic). Give it a name (for example, Data viz), tick the repo scope, generate it, and copy it - GitHub only shows it once. Paste the token wherever RStudio asks for your password.

It will now appear as if your RStudio is re-starting; don’t be feared, this is what is supposed to be happening. Projects are temporary representations of your RStudio environment, so that you can work on different projects with different data to keep your work structure clear.
If you look in your Files pane, you will see that the folder was selected, which holds all the information that was on the GitHub repository.
If you look in your Environment pane, you can now see an extra tab called Git. You have now successfully cloned your repository and let Git track your changes!


Step 2: Configure Git (only the first time)
Git needs to know who you are, so it can keep track of who made which changes. You only have to do this once per computer. Go to the Terminal tab in RStudio and type the following commands (replace <your-name> and <your-email> with your actual name and the email address that you use for GitHub):
git config --global user.email "<your-email>"
git config --global user.name "<your-name>"
Enter each command separately. The lines should be entered exactly like this, including the quotation marks, and you should see no output after entering the commands.

title: Working with Git
section: Now you can work in your project
text:
Now you can work in your project
Open this project whenever you are working on the group assignments. You do this by either clicking on the Project: <your-repo-name> button in the top right corner, or by double-clicking the .Rproj file in your project directory.
Commit, push, and pull changes via the terminal in RStudio, in the tab called Git, or in GitHub Desktop if you have that downloaded.
A few habits to enforce:

Pull before you start working, every single time (git pull, or the ⬇ button in the Git tab) — even if you were “just working on it five minutes ago.” A groupmate may have pushed since.
Commit small and often, with messages that say what changed ("add school-provider tidying step", not "updates"). Small commits are much easier to understand — and undo — than one giant one at the end.
Push when you’re done working, don’t sit on local changes overnight.

Close the project when you’re done working, to avoid accidentally making changes to the wrong project the next time you open RStudio.

Coordinate on who’s editing what. With a small group, it’s usually enough to communicate with each other to decide who is working in which script/document. Two people editing the same file at the same time is the main thing that causes trouble. Tip: If you do want to work on different versions of the same code, create subfolders with your names, and duplicate the code from the main folder that you want to edit. That way, you work “locally”, then decide together on the final code.

You do not need feature branches for a project this size — working directly on main, carefully, is simpler and easier to reason about for a two-week group project.

title: Working with Git
section: If you do get a merge conflict
text:
If you do get a merge conflict
It’s not a disaster — git is telling you it found two different versions of the same lines and needs you to pick. Open the file; git marks the conflicting section like this:
<<<<<<< HEAD
your version
=======
your groupmate's version
>>>>>>> their-commit
Decide (with them, if it’s not obvious) which lines should stay, delete the <<<<<<</=======/>>>>>>> markers, save the file, then git add it and finish the commit. Ask for help if you’re stuck!

text:
Part 1: Research question and exploration
The goal of Part 1 is to get your project off the ground: by the end of the first week, your group should have a clear research question, a working project setup, and a first look at the data. Part 1 is graded as complete / incomplete: we don’t grade the quality of your plot, but use it to give you feedback on your ideas early on.

A. Specify your research question
Together with your group, read the instructions for your research question in Research Questions below. If you choose RQ5, formulate your own research question as described there.

Does your project take an analytical, inference, or predictive approach (see Levels of visualization)? Is it clear what is expected in the final data visualization with regards to the approach?

Who is your target audience? How might this influence choices for your final visualization?



B. Set up your project and load the data
For this project, you will collaborate using Git. Set up your group’s repository from the starter project, and connect it to RStudio by following the instructions in Working with Git. If this is done correctly, the resulting repository should have the following folder structure:

├── .gitignore

What is the structure of the data?

What data cleaning steps are necessary? Do you, for example, need to filter out some observations to obtain reliable results?

use multiple plots
change the theme (you can use a default theme or create your own)
use a good color-scheme, for example colorblind proof

The report
You will write the assignment in R Markdown (or Quarto), to produce a report-style document of no more than 1000 words. The final version should be compiled into .html format.
The report should be a description of the process that led to your final data visualization. You should include:

However, we will grade the quality of the report as a whole, which includes communication about how the exploratory graph helped you to understand the data, and influenced your choices for the final, explanatory, data visualization.

Grading
The final report will be graded on the following elements:

Aesthetics [30%]: The overall visual quality of the plot. Is it clear and legible, with no unnecessary clutter? Do choices like color, labels, or scales enhance readability and interpretation?
Communication [30%]: How well the visualization conveys its intended message. Can the main point be understood quickly with minimal explanation? Do the title, labels, and layout support effective communication?
Description [20%]: The quality of the written report. Does it clearly state the research question, what you wanted to communicate, and why this visualization is appropriate? Does it provide a concise interpretation of what can be concluded from the data? Is it explanatory?
Creativity and Complexity [10%]: The thoughtfulness and depth of the visualization. Does it go beyond a default chart type when appropriate? Were creative or more complex techniques used in a way that adds value without obscuring the message?
Code Quality and Styling [10%]: The clarity and reproducibility of the R code. Does the code run without errors and generate the submitted plot? Is it well-structured, readable, and consistent with good style practices (i.e., lintr-proof)?

title: DV Assignment 2 (Group Project)
text:
Levels of visualization
Your chosen research question falls into one of three levels: analytics, inference, or prediction. Each level has different expectations in terms of how the visualization should be constructed and what role statistical modeling plays.

Analytics
Analytics is about describing and comparing what is happening in the data, often in a way that is directly actionable for a practitioner. At this level, we expect you to create clear, actionable visualizations that are easy to interpret for a practitioner (e.g. a school board or municipal education officer). This should rely less on statistical modeling and more on effective communication of patterns in the data. You do, however, need to make sure that the patterns communicated are reliable.


Inference
Inference goes one step further: it aims to explain differences or relationships in the data, often by comparing groups or testing hypotheses. We expect a visualization at this level to be supplemented with statistical tests or models (e.g. significance tests). The visualization should not only show patterns but also provide evidence for why the observed differences matter.


Prediction
Prediction focuses on using current information to forecast outcomes. At this level, you should fit and interpret a predictive model (e.g., a linear or logistic regression). The visualization should clearly communicate how well the model performs, what predictors matter, and what can be learned from the model’s outcomes.

title: DV Assignment 2 (Group Project)
text:
Data and codebook
All research questions use the DUO open data that you already worked with in the worksheets: eindscores, referentieniveaus, schooladviezen and schoolweging. Start from the starter project: its scripts/01-get-data.R downloads and loads all four files.

The data: background & codebook explains where the data comes from, the fairness debate these questions come from, every column in the four files, and the Dutch terms you’ll run into (reference levels, school advice tracks, schoolweging).







Hidden counts: "<5"





DUO hides any count below 5 and writes the text "<5" instead. In referentieniveaus and schooladviezen this happens a lot, because students are split over many small categories. If you simply drop the schools with a "<5" somewhere, almost no schools are left over.
The code below therefore replaces "<5" with a number of your choice (2.5, the midpoint of 1–4, by default). This is an assumption, so check whether your conclusion changes when you use 1 or 4 instead, and report this in your robustness section.



Run the chunk below first, whichever research question you choose. It loads the data and creates the helper objects that the RQ-specific chunks use.


Data preparation (all RQs):
# Load packages and data. Run this from your own project (the starter
# template): 01-get-data.R downloads the data if needed, and loads
# eindscores, referentieniveaus, schooladviezen and schoolweging.
source(here::here("scripts", "00-packages.R"))
source(here::here("scripts", "01-get-data.R"))

# DUO writes "<5" for counts under 5. This helper turns a count column into
# numbers, replacing "<5" with `value`. Rerun your analysis with 1 and 4 to
# check that your conclusion doesn't depend on this choice.
suppressed_value <- 2.5

parse_count <- function(x, value = suppressed_value) {
  x <- as.character(x)
  as.numeric(replace(x, x == "<5", value))
}

# Which test provider did each school use? Only eindscores has this. Most
# schools use one provider; for the few that use more, we keep the provider
# that tested the most students.
school_provider <- eindscores |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = ends_with("_AANTAL"),
    names_to = "provider",
    values_to = "n_tested"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    provider = str_remove(provider, "_AANTAL"),
    n_tested = parse_count(n_tested)
  ) |>
  filter(n_tested > 0) |>
  slice_max(
    n_tested,
    by = c(INSTELLINGSCODE, VESTIGINGSCODE),
    with_ties = FALSE
  ) |>
  select(INSTELLINGSCODE, VESTIGINGSCODE, provider, n_tested)

# Schoolweging per school. OVT combines INSTELLINGSCODE and a location code
# (e.g. "00AP|C1"), so we split it and summarise per INSTELLINGSCODE, which
# is what we can join on (see the comments at the bottom of 01-get-data.R).
school_weging <- schoolweging |>
  separate_wider_delim(
    OVT,
    delim = "|",
    names = c("INSTELLINGSCODE", "location")
  ) |>
  summarise(
    schoolweging = weighted.mean(schoolweging, aantal_leerlingen),
    spreiding = weighted.mean(spreiding, aantal_leerlingen),
    n_students_school = sum(aantal_leerlingen),
    .by = INSTELLINGSCODE
  )

# Reference levels: share of students per school reaching each level.
# Maths (REKENEN): basic level 1F, target level 1S.
# Reading (LV, leesvaardigheid): basic level 1F, target level 2F.
ref_levels <- referentieniveaus |>
  mutate(across(REKENEN_LAGER1F:TV_2F, parse_count)) |>
  mutate(
    n_maths = REKENEN_LAGER1F + REKENEN_1F + REKENEN_1S + REKENEN_2F,
    pct_maths_1f = 1 - REKENEN_LAGER1F / n_maths,
    pct_maths_1s = (REKENEN_1S + REKENEN_2F) / n_maths,
    n_reading = LV_LAGER1F + LV_1F + LV_2F,
    pct_reading_1f = 1 - LV_LAGER1F / n_reading,
    pct_reading_2f = LV_2F / n_reading
  )

# School advice: number of students per secondary-school track, plus the share
# of students with a HAVO-or-higher advice (you may define this differently!)
advice <- schooladviezen |>
  mutate(across(VSO:ADVIES_NIET_MOGELIJK, parse_count)) |>
  mutate(
    n_advice = rowSums(pick(VSO:ADVIES_NIET_MOGELIJK)),
    pct_havo_plus = (HAVO + HAVO_VWO + VWO) / n_advice
  )

title: DV Assignment 2 (Group Project)
text:
Research Questions

RQ1. Which schools in a municipality are on track for reading and maths?


Expand Instructions


Level: Analytics
Target audience: a municipal education officer or a school board.
Instruction: Choose one municipality, and visualize how each of its primary schools performs on the reference levels for maths (1F and 1S) and reading (1F and 2F). The visualization should be useful for the municipality: they should be able to see at a glance which schools are on track and which are falling behind. You can choose one of two ways to define “on track”:

National benchmark: compare each school to the national average share of students reaching each level.
Comparable-schools benchmark: compare each school to schools with a similar student population, i.e. a similar schoolweging. A school with many disadvantaged students and 40% at 1S may be doing better than expected, while a school with very few disadvantaged students and the same 40% may not be.

Good municipalities to start with are Haarlem (38 schools), Leiden (25) or Delft (25). Larger cities like Amsterdam (200+ schools) are possible, but you will need to think harder about how to keep the plot readable.


Data:
# Run the data preparation chunk above first.

# Choose your municipality (see unique(ref_levels$GEMEENTENAAM))
my_municipality <- "Haarlem"

# National benchmark: average share per level across all schools
national <- ref_levels |>
  summarise(across(starts_with("pct_"), \(x) mean(x, na.rm = TRUE)))

# Reference levels of the schools in your municipality, with schoolweging
rq1_data <- ref_levels |>
  filter(GEMEENTENAAM == my_municipality) |>
  left_join(school_weging, by = "INSTELLINGSCODE") |>
  select(
    INSTELLINGSCODE, VESTIGINGSCODE, INSTELLINGSNAAM_VESTIGING,
    n_maths, pct_maths_1f, pct_maths_1s,
    n_reading, pct_reading_1f, pct_reading_2f,
    schoolweging
  )








Tip






Some schools only have 10–15 students in group 8. How reliable is a percentage based on so few students, and how does the "<5" replacement affect small schools in particular? (How) will you show this in your visualization?
Almost every school gets (nearly) all students to the basic 1F level. Which levels are actually informative for telling schools apart?
You do not need to worry about generalizability to other municipalities. The visualization should be relevant for this one municipality.








RQ2. Does the choice of test provider matter, even for schools with a similar student population?


Expand Instructions


Level: Inference
Target audience: policymakers, or the general public (think of a newspaper graphic).
Instruction: Schools can choose which of six providers’ doorstroomtoets their students take. The Volkskrant reported that schools using some providers get structurally better results than comparable schools using another provider. In this RQ, you will test whether you can find the same in the DUO data.
The raw test scores (*_GEM in eindscores) are on six different scales and can’t be compared across providers. Use the reference levels instead: they are meant to mean the same thing regardless of which test a student took. Choose one or more of the following outcomes:

pct_maths_1s: share of students reaching the maths target level
pct_reading_2f: share of students reaching the reading target level

Compare these between providers, while accounting for schoolweging – schools do not choose their provider at random, so a raw comparison between providers is misleading. Support your visualization with a statistical model (e.g. a linear regression with provider and schoolweging as predictors).


Data:
# Run the data preparation chunk above first.

# Reference levels per school, with the school's provider and schoolweging
rq2_data <- ref_levels |>
  inner_join(school_provider, by = c("INSTELLINGSCODE", "VESTIGINGSCODE")) |>
  left_join(school_weging, by = "INSTELLINGSCODE") |>
  # AMN and DOE are used by too few schools to compare reliably
  filter(provider %in% c("LIB", "IEP", "ROUTE8", "DIA")) |>
  select(
    INSTELLINGSCODE, VESTIGINGSCODE, INSTELLINGSNAAM_VESTIGING,
    GEMEENTENAAM, PROVINCIE, provider,
    n_maths, pct_maths_1s, n_reading, pct_reading_2f,
    schoolweging
  )








Tip






First look at the raw differences between providers, then at the differences for schools with a similar schoolweging. Does the picture change? This comparison could be the core of your story.
A statistically significant difference is not necessarily a large one. How big are the differences, in terms your audience understands (e.g. “x more students per class of 25”)?
This is school-level data: you know which provider a school used, not the scores of individual students. What can and can’t you conclude from that?








RQ3. Do schools with similar test results give similar secondary-school advice?


Expand Instructions


Level: Inference
Target audience: secondary schools, or policymakers.
Instruction: At the end of primary school, every student receives a school advice for a secondary-school track (PRO, VMBO, HAVO, VWO, see the codebook). The advice is based on the teacher’s judgement and on the doorstroomtoets. In this RQ, you will investigate how closely a school’s advice follows its students’ test results, and whether this differs between schools with a more or less disadvantaged student population.
Relate a measure of the school’s advice (e.g. pct_havo_plus) to a measure of its test results (pct_maths_1s and/or pct_reading_2f), and test whether schoolweging moderates this relationship (e.g. with an interaction in a linear regression). Do two schools with the same results give the same advice, regardless of who their students are?


Data:
# Run the data preparation chunk above first.

# Test results and school advice per school, with schoolweging
rq3_data <- ref_levels |>
  inner_join(
    select(
      advice,
      INSTELLINGSCODE, VESTIGINGSCODE,
      VSO:ADVIES_NIET_MOGELIJK, n_advice, pct_havo_plus
    ),
    by = c("INSTELLINGSCODE", "VESTIGINGSCODE")
  ) |>
  left_join(school_weging, by = "INSTELLINGSCODE") |>
  select(
    INSTELLINGSCODE, VESTIGINGSCODE, INSTELLINGSNAAM_VESTIGING,
    GEMEENTENAAM, PROVINCIE,
    n_maths, pct_maths_1s, n_reading, pct_reading_2f,
    VSO:ADVIES_NIET_MOGELIJK, n_advice, pct_havo_plus,
    schoolweging
  )








Tip






pct_havo_plus is only one way to summarise the advice. You could also turn the tracks into a numeric scale (PRO = 1, …, VWO = 6) and compute an average advice per school. Argue your choice.
Suppose you find that schools with a higher schoolweging give lower advice than schools with the same test results. What are possible explanations? Is it necessarily unfair? Discuss this in your report.








RQ4. Can we predict how many students get a HAVO-or-higher advice from a school’s context?


Expand Instructions


Level: Prediction
Target audience: school boards or the Inspectorate, who could use such a model to spot schools whose advice is unexpectedly high or low.
Instruction: Fit a model that predicts a school’s share of students with a HAVO-or-higher advice (pct_havo_plus) from characteristics of the school and its student population. Deliberately leave out the test results themselves (the reference levels): we want to know how much the context alone predicts. You can choose between the following predictors:

schoolweging (how disadvantaged the student population is)
spreiding (how much the students within a school differ from each other in disadvantage)
n_students_school (school size)
provider (which doorstroomtoets the school used)
PROVINCIE
DENOMINATIE_VESTIGING (the school’s religious or educational denomination)

You can be selective or choose all variables. If you choose to omit certain variables, please explain why. Evaluate your model on data it hasn’t seen (e.g. a train/test split) and communicate how well it performs, which predictors matter, and which schools deviate most from what the model predicts.


Data:
# Run the data preparation chunk above first.

# School advice per school, with school context and provider
rq4_data <- advice |>
  left_join(school_weging, by = "INSTELLINGSCODE") |>
  left_join(school_provider, by = c("INSTELLINGSCODE", "VESTIGINGSCODE")) |>
  # special primary schools (Sbo) have no schoolweging
  filter(SOORT_PO == "Bo") |>
  select(
    INSTELLINGSCODE, VESTIGINGSCODE, INSTELLINGSNAAM_VESTIGING,
    GEMEENTENAAM, PROVINCIE, DENOMINATIE_VESTIGING,
    n_advice, pct_havo_plus,
    schoolweging, spreiding, n_students_school, provider
  )








Tip






DENOMINATIE_VESTIGING has 19 categories and some providers are rare. Categories with only a handful of schools make your model unstable – consider combining them.
A school with 8 students in group 8 will have a much noisier pct_havo_plus than a school with 80. How do you deal with that in your model, or in your visualization?
A school that deviates from the model’s prediction is not necessarily doing something wrong. Keep this in mind when you present the “outliers”.








RQ5. Your own research question


Expand Instructions


Level: Your choice (analytics, inference or prediction)
Instruction: If none of the questions above appeal to you, you can formulate your own. The DUO data should be the core of your project, but you are welcome to combine it with other data. This option gives you more freedom, but it also asks more of you: you have to make the choices that RQ1–RQ4 make for you. Before you start working on the data, make sure you have specified the following:

A very specific research question. “Is the doorstroomtoets fair?” is a topic, not a research question. A good question names the outcome, the comparison and the population, so that it’s clear which plot and which analysis would answer it. For example: “Do schools in Limburg that use Route 8 have a lower share of students at reading level 2F than Route 8 schools in the rest of the country, when comparing schools with a similar schoolweging?”
An approach. Is your question one of analytics, inference or prediction (see Levels of visualization)? Explain why, and what statistical test or model (if any) you will use to support your visualization.
A target audience. Who is your visualization for, and what should they be able to do or conclude after seeing it? This shapes your choices just as much as the data does.

State all three explicitly at the start of your report.
Adding other data. You can look for other data to combine with the DUO files, for example DUO data from other school years (to look at changes over time), neighbourhood statistics from CBS (Statistics Netherlands), or geographic data to make a map. The school codes (INSTELLINGSCODE, VESTIGINGSCODE), postcode (POSTCODE_VESTIGING) and municipality (GEMEENTENAAM, GEMEENTENUMMER) are the columns you can use to join other data to the DUO files.
We recommend using AI tools to help you with this: to sharpen your question, to find datasets that could answer it, and to figure out how to join them to the DUO data. But check what AI gives you. Make sure a dataset actually exists and comes from a trustworthy source, check how many schools actually match after joining (and which ones don’t), and describe in your report which data you used, where it comes from, and how you combined it.


Data:
# Run the data preparation chunk above first. Then start from whichever of
# the prepared objects fits your question (ref_levels, advice,
# school_provider, school_weging), or from the raw DUO files.

# If you add other data, download it in a script (like 01-get-data.R) so
# that your project stays reproducible, and save it in data/raw/ -- never
# push data to GitHub.








Tip






Keep it small. A narrow question that you answer well is better than a broad question that you answer superficially.
Before you commit to a question, check that the data can actually answer it: are the variables you need there, and are there enough schools in each group you want to compare?

title: Data Visualization Assignment 1
text:
Getting the data
This assignment uses real, public data about the doorstroomtoets - the standardized test Dutch primary school pupils take in their final year (groep 8), which feeds into their secondary-school advice. Before starting, read data/doorstroomtoetsen-context.md in the course repository for the background on why this data is interesting (it’s the subject of an active public debate about fairness), and data/data-context.md for a glossary of the Dutch terms you’ll run into plus a full codebook of every column in the data files below - useful if you’re not familiar with the Dutch education system or language.
Download get-data.R from the course GitHub repository and run it once in your project folder - it downloads everything this assignment needs into data/raw/.

title: Data Visualization Assignment 1
text:
Part 1: Doorstroomtoets Data & Basic ggplot (Individual)

A. Replicate this plot
The following code will give you the data necessary to create the plot at the end of this section. Your task is to replicate the plot using ggplot2.
Don’t worry if you cannot reproduce the plots exactly. You can, for example, use different colors and font families.
Grading:

Does the data show the same pattern? [2 pt]
Is the styling the same? [2 pt]
BONUS: Was a meaningful explanatory element added to one of the plots? [0.5 pt]

Bonus points
Every plot in this assignment shows the data accurately, but none of them explains itself - a reader still has to do some work to find the result that matters most. For the bonus point, add ONE explanatory element to either plot that helps a reader find that result faster. Simply changing colors or a theme will not be rewarded on its own, unless it’s clearly in service of highlighting a specific result. See the Solution below for a list of ideas if you’re stuck.

knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE) # set default echo = TRUE for all code blocks
rm(list = ls()) # Remove any existing objects in memory


# Install Packages
all_installed_packages <- installed.packages()[, "Package"]
# nolint start -- trick to omit some lines from the lintr checker, only if you have a good reason!
if (!"tidyverse" %in% all_installed_packages) {
  install.packages("tidyverse")
}
if (!"cowplot" %in% all_installed_packages) {
  install.packages("cowplot")
}
if (!"readODS" %in% all_installed_packages) {
  install.packages("readODS")
}
if (!"lintr" %in% all_installed_packages) {
  install.packages("lintr")
}
# nolint end

library(tidyverse)
library(cowplot)
library(readODS)

For this assignment, we look at the doorstroomtoets results published by DUO, alongside two other public files: the reference-level attainment per school, and the school weighting (“schoolweging” - a school-level disadvantage score) published by the Education Inspectorate.

eindscores <- read_delim(
  "data/raw/eindscores_2024-2025.csv",
  delim = ";", locale = locale(decimal_mark = ",", encoding = "UTF-8"),
  show_col_types = FALSE
)

referentieniveaus <- read_delim(
  "data/raw/referentieniveaus_2024-2025.csv",
  delim = ";", quote = '"', show_col_types = FALSE
)

schoolweging_raw <- read_ods(
  "data/raw/schoolweging_2022-2025.ods",
  sheet = "2024-2025"
)

Now that we have the “raw” data, we can start to filter and prepare it. eindscores has one row per school with a pair of columns per test provider (IEP_AANTAL/IEP_GEM, and so on) - we need one row per (school, provider actually used) instead, so we pivot_longer() those pairs.

school_provider <- eindscores |>
  select(INSTELLINGSCODE, matches("_(AANTAL|GEM)$")) |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = matches("_(AANTAL|GEM)$"),
    names_to = c("provider", ".value"),
    names_pattern = "(.+)_(AANTAL|GEM)"
  ) |>
  # DUO writes "<5" for small counts -> NA
  mutate(AANTAL = as.numeric(AANTAL)) |>
  filter(!is.na(AANTAL), AANTAL > 0, !is.na(GEM), GEM > 0) |>
  group_by(INSTELLINGSCODE, provider) |>
  summarise(AANTAL = sum(AANTAL), .groups = "drop")

# most schools only use one provider - take whichever tested the most pupils
primary_provider <- school_provider |>
  group_by(INSTELLINGSCODE) |>
  slice_max(AANTAL, n = 1, with_ties = FALSE) |>
  ungroup() |>
  select(INSTELLINGSCODE, provider)

Next, the school weighting. That file identifies schools slightly differently (an OVT column like "00AP|C1" instead of separate INSTELLINGSCODE/VESTIGINGSCODE columns), so a bit of string splitting is needed before it can be joined to anything else.

schoolweging <- schoolweging_raw |>
  mutate(INSTELLINGSCODE = str_remove(OVT, "\\|.*$")) |>
  group_by(INSTELLINGSCODE) |>
  summarise(
    schoolweging = weighted.mean(schoolweging, w = aantal_leerlingen),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

Finally, the outcome we’ll actually plot. Raw scores aren’t comparable across providers (an IEP score and an AMN score are not the same kind of number), but the percentage of pupils reaching the target reference level (1S for maths, 2F for language) is - that’s the one number CvTE’s shared framework is designed to make provider-independent.

count_cols <- c(
  "REKENEN_LAGER1F", "REKENEN_1F", "REKENEN_1S",
  "LV_LAGER1F", "LV_1F", "LV_2F",
  "TV_LAGER1F", "TV_1F", "TV_2F"
)

ref_levels <- referentieniveaus |>
  mutate(across(all_of(count_cols), ~ suppressWarnings(as.numeric(.)))) |>
  group_by(INSTELLINGSCODE) |>
  summarise(
    across(all_of(count_cols), ~ sum(.x, na.rm = TRUE)),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    rekenen_n = REKENEN_LAGER1F + REKENEN_1F + REKENEN_1S,
    taal_lv_n = LV_LAGER1F + LV_1F + LV_2F,
    taal_tv_n = TV_LAGER1F + TV_1F + TV_2F,
    score = (
      100 * REKENEN_1S / rekenen_n +
        100 * LV_2F / taal_lv_n +
        100 * TV_2F / taal_tv_n
    ) / 3,
    n_pupils = rekenen_n
  ) |>
  filter(rekenen_n > 0, taal_lv_n > 0, taal_tv_n > 0) |>
  select(INSTELLINGSCODE, score, n_pupils)

school_data <- ref_levels |>
  inner_join(primary_provider, by = "INSTELLINGSCODE") |>
  left_join(schoolweging, by = "INSTELLINGSCODE")

Now we can make the first plot: an overlapping density curve of every school’s score, one per provider, for LIB, IEP and Route8. geom_density() normalizes each curve to its own area, so LIB (far more schools behind it) and Route8 stay comparable on shape. I used these settings in my rMarkdown code chunk: fig.height = 5, fig.width = 5.5, fig.align = "center"

For the second plot, take those same three providers, plus the national average, and check whether their gap survives once you’re comparing schools with the same school weighting. Give the three providers a proper legend, with each provider’s total pupil count included in the label (e.g. "LIB (n = 71,120)") - so a reader can see at a glance how much data is actually behind each line. The national average doesn’t belong in that legend (it isn’t “a test”), so it gets no points and no legend entry - just its own dashed line, labeled directly on the plot with a small geom_label() layer built from a separate, one-row data frame. I used these settings in my rMarkdown code chunk: fig.height = 5, fig.width = 5.5, fig.align = "center"

Finally we make a plot with text, to state in words what both panels show together. I used these settings in my rMarkdown code chunk: fig.height = 2, fig.width = 11.5, fig.align = "center"

Finally we combine the three plots (one text plot and two figure plots) into one plot by means of the plot_grid function of the cowplot package. This is the visualization that you should replicate in this assignment. Notice that the density plot’s legend is gone in the combined version - once plot 2 has its own legend naming the same three providers, a second legend for plot 1 would just repeat it.
I used these settings in my rMarkdown code chunk: fig.height = 6, fig.width = 11.5, fig.align = "center"

PlotSolution






Plot 1:

highlighted_providers <- c("LIB", "IEP", "ROUTE8")
provider_colors <- c(LIB = "#2a78d6", IEP = "#eb6834", ROUTE8 = "#1baf7a")

school_data_3 <- school_data |>
  filter(provider %in% highlighted_providers)

# color for the national average line/label in plot 2
national_color <- "grey35"

plot1 <- ggplot(
  school_data_3,
  aes(x = score, fill = provider, color = provider)
) +
  geom_density(alpha = 0.45, linewidth = 0.2, color = "white") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = provider_colors, name = "Test provider") +
  scale_color_manual(values = provider_colors, guide = "none") +
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(0, 100)) +
  labs(x = "% of students reaching target level, per school", y = "Density") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(panel.grid.minor = element_blank(), legend.position = "bottom")
plot(plot1)



Plot 2:

plotted_schools <- school_data |>
  filter(provider %in% highlighted_providers, !is.na(schoolweging)) |>
  mutate(weging_bin = floor(schoolweging / 2) * 2) |>
  filter(weging_bin >= 22, weging_bin <= 38) # drop the near-empty tail bins

provider_lines <- plotted_schools |>
  group_by(provider, weging_bin) |>
  summarise(score = weighted.mean(score, w = n_pupils), .groups = "drop")

# one row per weging_bin, averaging across all three providers together -
# this is the dashed "national average" line
national_line <- plotted_schools |>
  group_by(weging_bin) |>
  summarise(score = weighted.mean(score, w = n_pupils), .groups = "drop")
national_label <- national_line |>
  filter(weging_bin == max(weging_bin))

# how many pupils sit behind each provider's line - shown in the legend
# labels below
provider_n <- plotted_schools |>
  group_by(provider) |>
  summarise(n_pupils = sum(n_pupils), .groups = "drop")

legend_labels <- setNames(
  paste0(
    provider_n$provider,
    " \n(n = ",
    format(provider_n$n_pupils, big.mark = ","),
    ")"
  ),
  provider_n$provider
)

# the first and last point of each provider's line
provider_ends <- provider_lines |>
  group_by(provider) |>
  filter(weging_bin %in% range(weging_bin)) |>
  ungroup()

plot2 <- ggplot() +
  geom_line(
    data = national_line, aes(x = weging_bin, y = score),
    color = national_color, linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 0.9
  ) +
  geom_label(
    data = national_label, aes(
      x = weging_bin,
      y = score,
      label = "National average"
    ),
    color = national_color, fill = "white", linewidth = 0, hjust = 0,
    size = 3.2, fontface = "italic"
  ) +
  geom_line(
    data = provider_lines,
    aes(x = weging_bin, y = score, color = provider),
    linewidth = 1.1
  ) +
  geom_point(
    data = provider_ends,
    aes(x = weging_bin, y = score, color = provider),
    size = 3,
    show.legend = FALSE
  ) +
  scale_color_manual(
    values = provider_colors,
    labels = legend_labels,
    name = "Test provider"
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(21, 42), breaks = seq(22, 38, 4)) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 100)) +
  labs(
    x = "School weighting (higher = more disadvantaged)",
    y = "% reaching target level"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(panel.grid.minor = element_blank(), legend.position = "top")
plot(plot2)



Plot 3:

# plain text, not built from the data - the two plots already show the
# numbers; the title states the conclusion in words
title_text <- paste(
  "LIB has the highest percentage of students reaching the target level,",
  "and Route8 the lowest. This gap holds even when accounting for the",
  "socio-economic status of schools."
)

title_plot <- ggplot() +
  annotate("text",
    x = 0, y = 0, label = str_wrap(title_text, width = 105),
    size = 6, fontface = "bold", family = "Times", hjust = 0.5
  ) +
  theme_void()
plot(title_plot)



Combined:

# plot1 keeps its legend when shown on its own (above), but not here: with
# plot2's legend right next to it, a second one for plot1 would just repeat
# the same three names
plot1_no_legend <- plot1 + theme(legend.position = "none")

bottom_row <- suppressMessages(plot_grid(plot1_no_legend, plot2))
combined <- suppressWarnings(
  plot_grid(title_plot, bottom_row, ncol = 1, rel_heights = c(1, 3))
)
print(combined)



Bonus
The bonus point (0.5 pt) is for adding one meaningful explanatory element to either plot - something that helps a reader find the result that matters without reading the code. Some ideas, if you’re stuck (pick one, don’t do all of them):

Show only the highest- and lowest-performing provider, and highlight the difference between them directly (e.g. a bracket, a shaded gap, or a labeled arrow spanning it).
Add text and/or an arrow that points at the specific part of the plot it’s explaining, rather than a caption floating nearby with no visual connection.
Use color and/or opacity (alpha) to pull one specific result forward, paired with a short written conclusion about what it means.
Add a title to a sub-plot - but only if it says something the shared title above doesn’t already say.
Mark a “risk zone”: a shaded band flagging where a result crosses into concerning territory (e.g. a score below some minimum standard).
Plot 2 already has a reference/benchmark line (the national average, via geom_line() + a geom_label() with fill = "white" and linewidth = 0 so it reads over the line without a visible box border). Plot 1 doesn’t have anything like it yet - could it? (A single geom_vline() at the pooled average score, since plot 1’s x-axis is already the score itself, is one way in.)
Label a specific data point directly with its value, instead of making the reader read it off the axis.
Flag where the data is thin (e.g. Route8 has far fewer schools behind it at high school weighting) so a reader doesn’t over-trust the wobbliest part of a line.





Tips:

geom_density() is already normalized to area = 1 per group by default - that’s what keeps LIB’s ~2,600 schools and Route8’s ~300 comparable on shape without you having to do anything extra.
Read data/doorstroomtoetsen-context.md section 7 and data/data-context.md before you start - they’ve already profiled this exact dataset (missingness, provider market share, the "<5" suppression convention, and what every column/Dutch term means) and will save you re-discovering the same gotchas.
To pick good colors, use node scripts/validate_palette.js from the dataviz skill (or http://colorbrewer2.org) rather than eyeballing whether two colors are colorblind-safe.



B. Interactive visualizations with Plotly
Copy the code below to prepare the data - the same kind of school-level dataset as Part A, but keeping every provider (not just the three highlighted ones) and bringing in a school’s name, municipality and province, useful context for a tooltip but not something Part A’s plots needed.
Now, your assignment is to:

Build a scatterplot showing every school’s doorstroomtoets score against its school weighting - one point per school (only schools with 40 or more pupils tested, to avoid noisy small-sample scores), colored by which test provider it used, sized by how many pupils it tested. See the image below for what you’re aiming for.
Make this plot interactive using the the plotly package. Tip: You can use the ggplotly() function to convert a ggplot object to an interactive plotly object.
Add a tooltip that displays additional information when you hover over the plot. Customize the tooltip so that it displays the default plot values and additional insights from two other variables (choose yourself). Make sure all of this information is visible when you hover over the plot.

Grading:

Does the interactive plot work? [1 pt]
Does the tooltip clearly display additional (meaningful) information next to the default plot values? [1 pt]


library(tidyverse)
library(readODS)
library(plotly)


eindscores <- read_delim(
  "data/raw/eindscores_2024-2025.csv",
  delim = ";", locale = locale(decimal_mark = ",", encoding = "UTF-8"),
  show_col_types = FALSE
)

referentieniveaus <- read_delim(
  "data/raw/referentieniveaus_2024-2025.csv",
  delim = ";", quote = '"', show_col_types = FALSE
)

schoolweging_raw <- read_ods(
  "data/raw/schoolweging_2022-2025.ods",
  sheet = "2024-2025"
)

# one row per (school, provider actually used)
school_provider <- eindscores |>
  select(INSTELLINGSCODE, matches("_(AANTAL|GEM)$")) |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = matches("_(AANTAL|GEM)$"),
    names_to = c("provider", ".value"),
    names_pattern = "(.+)_(AANTAL|GEM)"
  ) |>
  # DUO writes "<5" for small counts -> NA
  mutate(AANTAL = as.numeric(AANTAL)) |>
  filter(!is.na(AANTAL), AANTAL > 0, !is.na(GEM), GEM > 0) |>
  group_by(INSTELLINGSCODE, provider) |>
  summarise(AANTAL = sum(AANTAL), .groups = "drop")

# one row per school: whichever single provider tested the most of its pupils
primary_provider <- school_provider |>
  group_by(INSTELLINGSCODE) |>
  slice_max(AANTAL, n = 1, with_ties = FALSE) |>
  ungroup() |>
  select(INSTELLINGSCODE, provider)

eindscores also carries the columns a tooltip needs later: a school’s name, province and municipality. Unlike province/municipality (always the same across a school’s locations), a school’s name sometimes isn’t - its different physical locations can have different names. Grouping by school code and taking just the first location’s row (name included) guarantees exactly one row per school, without silently duplicating any school whose locations disagree on a name.

school_location <- eindscores |>
  select(INSTELLINGSCODE, INSTELLINGSNAAM_VESTIGING, PROVINCIE, GEMEENTENAAM) |>
  group_by(INSTELLINGSCODE) |>
  slice(1) |>
  ungroup()

schoolweging <- schoolweging_raw |>
  mutate(INSTELLINGSCODE = str_remove(OVT, "\\|.*$")) |>
  group_by(INSTELLINGSCODE) |>
  summarise(
    schoolweging = weighted.mean(schoolweging, w = aantal_leerlingen),
    .groups = "drop"
  )


count_cols <- c(
  "REKENEN_LAGER1F", "REKENEN_1F", "REKENEN_1S",
  "LV_LAGER1F", "LV_1F", "LV_2F",
  "TV_LAGER1F", "TV_1F", "TV_2F"
)

ref_levels <- referentieniveaus |>
  mutate(across(all_of(count_cols), ~ suppressWarnings(as.numeric(.)))) |>
  group_by(INSTELLINGSCODE) |>
  summarise(
    across(all_of(count_cols), ~ sum(.x, na.rm = TRUE)),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    rekenen_n = REKENEN_LAGER1F + REKENEN_1F + REKENEN_1S,
    taal_lv_n = LV_LAGER1F + LV_1F + LV_2F,
    taal_tv_n = TV_LAGER1F + TV_1F + TV_2F,
    score = (
      100 * REKENEN_1S / rekenen_n +
        100 * LV_2F / taal_lv_n +
        100 * TV_2F / taal_tv_n
    ) / 3,
    n_pupils = rekenen_n
  ) |>
  filter(rekenen_n > 0, taal_lv_n > 0, taal_tv_n > 0) |>
  select(INSTELLINGSCODE, score, n_pupils)

# a school needs a known provider, a computable score, AND a schoolweging
# value to appear on this chart - unlike Part A's school_data, which kept
# schoolweging-less schools around for its density plot, this scatter has
# no use for a school it can't place on the x-axis
school_data <- ref_levels |>
  inner_join(primary_provider, by = "INSTELLINGSCODE") |>
  inner_join(school_location, by = "INSTELLINGSCODE") |>
  inner_join(schoolweging, by = "INSTELLINGSCODE") |>
  filter(!is.na(schoolweging))

Now it’s your turn! Build the scatterplot described above from school_data, then turn it into an interactive plotly object with a customized tooltip that shows additional context next to the default values when you hover over the plot.

PlotSolution






provider_colors <- c(
  LIB = "#2a78d6", IEP = "#eb6834", ROUTE8 = "#1baf7a",
  DIA = "#4a3aa7", AMN = "#e87ba4", DOE = "#eda100"
)

# only schools with a reasonably sized cohort - a school with a handful of
# pupils produces a very noisy score, not worth its own point on this chart
plot_data <- school_data |>
  filter(n_pupils >= 40)

plot_data_with_tooltip <- plot_data |>
  mutate(
    tooltip_text = paste0(
      "<b>", INSTELLINGSNAAM_VESTIGING, "</b>",
      "<br>", GEMEENTENAAM, ", ", PROVINCIE,
      "<br>Test provider: ", provider,
      "<br>School weighting: ", round(schoolweging, 1),
      "<br>% reaching target level: ", round(score, 1), "%",
      "<br>Pupils tested: ", n_pupils
    )
  )

interactive_plot <- ggplot(
  plot_data_with_tooltip,
  aes(x = schoolweging, y = score, color = provider, text = tooltip_text)
) +
  geom_point(aes(size = n_pupils), alpha = 0.5) +
  scale_color_manual(values = provider_colors) +
  labs(
    title = "Doorstroomtoets score by school weighting, per school",
    subtitle = "Showing schools with 40 or more students",
    x = "School weighting (higher = more disadvantaged)",
    y = "% reaching target level",
    color = "Test provider",
    size = "Number of Students"
  ) +
  theme_bw()

# tooltip = "text" - show ONLY the custom tooltip_text column on hover, not
# ggplotly's default (which would otherwise list every aesthetic separately:
# x, y, colour, size, text, all stacked in one ugly box)
ggplotly(interactive_plot, tooltip = "text") |>
  # nice trick to left align content in tooltip:
  layout(hoverlabel = list(align = "left"))

Full points were given for the interactive plot if the interactivity was working, and a tooltip with the two default variables plus two extra variables were added. If default or extra variables were missing, or if the tooltip was not formatted in a legible way, 0.5 pts were deducted.

A. Specify your research question
In class 1 you indicated your preference for a research question for the final project, and were assigned a group to work with. You were also assigned one of the GitHub repositories from the Oefenweb GitHub account, which you can use to collaborate on your research project. Together with your group, read the instructions for your assigned research question in Assignment 2 again.

Does your project take an analytical, inference, or predictive approach? Is it clear what is expected in the final data visualization with regards to the approach?

Who is your target audience? How might this influence choices for your final visualization?



B. Connect to Git and load data
For this project, you will collaborate using Git. Connect your server environment to GitHub and clone your assigned GitHub repository into your online RStudio account by following these instructions: Connecting RStudio Server to GitHub. If this is done correctly, the resulting repository should have the following folder structure:
your-project-name/
├── .gitignore
├── README.md

    └── DV-Assignment2-GroupX.html
All group members should clone the assigned group repository to their server environment. Once you have cloned the repo and initialized Git, make a first commit and push it. Check that the other group members can pull these changes. If this works, you should be properly set up to work together using Git!
Feel free to add folders or files within the repository if necessary. Make sure that you maintain the structure such that you follow a reproducible workflow. Additionally, it is important that you never push data to GitHub. If you have to store data, do this in a separate folder outside of your Git repository.
Now, load in the necessary data for your visualization. In the scripts/ folder, first run 00-packages.R to install and load all the packages you need, then run 01-get-data.R to download the data into data/raw/ and load it. Examine the data. Discuss with your group:

What is the structure of the data?

What are the main variables? Can you already make some exploratory plots to understand these variables better?

What data cleaning steps are necessary? Do you, for example, need to filter out some observations to obtain reliable results?



C. Make your first visualization
For this assignment you can make any visualization about the chosen theme of the final project with these minimal requirements:

use multiple plots
change the theme (you can use a default theme or create your own)
use a good color-scheme, for example colorblind proof
highlight some interesting data points, for example using color or text

Include a description of what you want to communicate, and how you did that. Really work towards making a data visualization that highlights or substantiates a single conclusion. This plot does not have to be the plot for your final project (it probably is not), but use this assignment to get feedback from us on your current ideas.

Is the plot simple? [0.5 pt]

The plot requires minimal explanation [0.5 pt]

Creative/complexity

Is the plot creative? [0.5 pt]

title: Working with AI
text:
Why this worksheet?
AI can now make a polished chart in seconds. A chart is no longer hard to make, so the hard part is knowing whether it is right: whether the data means what the chart suggests, and whether the conclusion holds.
Your role changes from building static visualizations to curating a generative system. The AI builds, but you set its parameters (the question, the data, the transformations, the audience, the claim) and you judge what it produces. You are responsible for every chart you hand in, including the ones AI made.
A visualization carries a message about data to people who usually can’t check that message themselves. This makes data literacy more important than ever. As behavioral data scientists, you bring something the AI does not have: knowledge of psychology, statistics, and the data at hand.

title: Working with AI
text:
Five guiding principles

1. You are the data scientist; the AI is your assistant
The AI can write code and produce charts. It cannot tell you whether any of it makes sense. That depends on conceptual knowledge only you can bring:

Meaning: what does this variable actually measure? What does a transfer-test score represent (and what does it not)?
Validity: does this data suit the real-world phenomenon it is supposed to represent? Is “average score per school” a good way to measure whether a test is fair?
Conclusion: is this visualization leading to a conclusion that is understandable, meaningful, and applicable?

If you can’t answer these questions yourself, the AI’s answer doesn’t help you. You have no way to know whether it is right.


2. Shape the data, shape the thinking
Every chart starts with decisions about the data, made before any plotting (Bertini):

Variable selection: which columns are in, which are left out?
Summary statistics: counts, means, medians? Means over what?
Filtering and ranges: which schools or years are dropped, and why?
Granularity: pupil, school, municipality, province?

AI makes these decisions silently and confidently. Each one affects what your reader will conclude. Ask the AI to list every transformation it made, and check each one.

DUO example: the *_AANTAL columns contain the string "<5" for privacy reasons. An AI that runs as.numeric() turns these into NA and drops them without telling you. What does that do to small schools, and to which providers?



3. Beware the illusion of causality
A clean chart with two variables that move together looks like an explanation. AI tools, and your readers, readily turn “goes together with” into “causes”.

DUO example: “Schools using test provider X have higher average scores.” Is that the test, or the kind of schools that choose that test? Check the school population (schoolweging) before writing the title.

Ask of every chart: what is the causal claim a naïve reader would take away, and do I actually have evidence for it?


4. Beware the illusion of simplicity
AI gives you a professional-looking chart for free. But polish is not substance: a chart can look finished while the data or analysis behind it is hollow (Ciuccarelli). AI can also produce a visual hallucination: a trend, cluster, or correlation that comes from a coding mistake, not from the data.

Don’t add elements (gradients, icons, annotations, 3D, interactivity) just because they are now cheap. Apply the data-to-ink ratio from Session 1.
A plain chart that is correct beats a beautiful chart that is wrong.



5. Curate, don’t just prompt
Define the parameters of the system before you ask it to build:

What is my question? What is my one conclusion?
Who is my audience, and what do they already know?
Which data, which transformations, and which comparison?
Which encodings, colors, and constraints (colorblind-safe, fits the report)?

Then evaluate what comes back against those parameters, not against “does it look good?”.
